brief: BofA argues the $40tn debt crossing did not cause the recent rise in long-end yields, because markets price changes in expected deficits and issuance rather than the level of debt, and no policy development shifted those expectations. It attributes the move to higher inflation expectations from energy prices and doubts about the Fed's price-stability commitment, partly quieted by Warsh at Jackson Hole. Higher rates still warrant fiscal focus: interest expense has run above $1.1tn (3.5% of GDP) over 12 months and now exceeds defense and Medicare, the 3.4% average rate on outstanding debt will reset roughly 1.4pp higher on refinancing, and 75bp of hikes adds about $50bn to bill costs. Higher interest costs raise deficits, deficits raise issuance, issuance raises term premium, which raises borrowing costs again. On policy, BofA expects 25bp hikes in September, October and December, with next week's August inflation data the decisive input. It forecasts core CPI at 0.22% m/m and core PCE at 0.24% m/m, enough to convince Warsh though below the roughly 0.30% bar Waller implied, while Williams signalled no need to hike. Labor data is soft but stable and 3Q GDP tracks 2.5%.
